title: Best Practices Are the Default
intro: Re-testing established best practices on every project wastes time and puts the burden of proof on the wrong person. Make the rule explicit.

learn.title: Flip the burden of proof
learn.text:
The common pattern: the researcher has to prove that icons need labels, that a scale works, that the convention applies here.

**Calabro's rule:** whoever wants to deviate from a well-evidenced practice brings the evidence.

Agreed once at a large tech company, the rule ended months of relitigating and improved outcomes across teams.

try.q: A stakeholder wants to ship icon-only navigation. Under Calabro's rule, who brings evidence?
options: The stakeholder proposing the deviation
The researcher who raised the concern
Whichever side has more stakeholders
Nobody — it should go straight to an A/B test
try.explain: The default is the evidenced practice; the exception has to prove itself.

left.label: Inverted (common)
items: Researcher must prove icons need labels

right.label: Fair (Calabro's rule)
items: Challenger brings data to skip labels
Use existing guidance and move on
Show the behaviour, not the belief

learn.title: Use your head about which research applies
learn.text:
In the 1990s, studies rated colour pairs **on swatches, out of context**. Sites adopted the “winning” palettes and many were unreadable.

A study of icon styles in isolation said little about icons in a real interface.

Some questions need not be asked. Some things need not be tested. And some findings don't transfer.

try.q: A study rates colour pairs on isolated swatches. What can you conclude for your product page?
options: Very little — the context is missing
That the winning pair will be most readable
That colour has no effect on readability
That the study should be repeated with more participants
try.explain: Context-free ratings didn't predict what worked on real pages.

learn.title: Before you cite a study
learn.text:
Check that it studied **your situation**: real interfaces, comparable users, comparable tasks.

The same discipline that protects you from re-testing the obvious also protects you from citing research that doesn't transfer.

try.q: What should you check before citing a study in a design argument?
options: Whether it studied a situation like yours
Whether it was published in the last two years
Whether the sample was at least 30 people
Whether its authors are well known in the industry
try.explain: Comparable interface, users and tasks — otherwise the finding doesn't transfer.

test.q: What is the default, in Calabro's rule?
options: The well-evidenced practice
Whatever the design system specifies
The option that tests fastest
The approach the previous team used
test.explain: Default to the evidence; make the exception prove itself.

test.q: What did the explicit rule achieve at the large tech company?
options: It ended months of relitigating the same debates
It reduced the research budget by a third
It replaced the need for a design system
It let the team ship without any usability testing
test.explain: And it improved outcomes across teams.

test.q: Why were the 1990s colour studies misleading?
options: Pairs were rated out of context, on swatches
The samples were too small to be meaningful
Monitors of the era showed colour inaccurately
Participants were all design professionals
test.explain: Sites adopted the winning palettes and many were unreadable.

test.q: “Our users are tech-savvy” is offered as a reason to skip labels. What does the rule ask for?
options: The behaviour, not the belief
A second opinion from another stakeholder
A written exception in the design system
A longer research timeline before deciding
test.explain: The claim needs evidence from those users.

test.q: Which is NOT a conclusion of this article?
options: Every best practice should be re-tested per project
Some questions need not be asked
Some findings don't transfer to your context
The challenger should bring the evidence
test.explain: Re-testing everything is exactly the waste it argues against.
